newsitem.title: USA: Florida at center stage in tobacco litigation.
newsitem.headline: Florida at center stage in tobacco litigation.

text.p: Last summer Florida gave the tobacco industry its worst courtroom bruising ever and stands ready and eager to bloody cigarette makers again in 1997.

Three big trials, including one on a huge state government claim, are set for Florida next year. Opposing lawyers' demands for documents, pretrial scuffling over technicalities and appeals have largely been settled. Juries will soon be chosen.
A class-action lawsuit, pulling together the claims of as many as 250,000 flight attendants with illnesses associated with inhaling secondhand smoke on passenger jets, is set for June in Miami.

A second Miami trial of a class action by people claiming they were addicted to cigarettes is set for September, and a multibillion-dollar lawsuit by the state of Florida meant to recoup medical costs for smokers covered by state health care programmes is to start in August in West Palm Beach.
"Florida is really on the cutting edge," said Professor Jean Eggen of the Widener University School of Law in Wilmington, Del. "Florida has more tobacco litigation than anywhere else."

Florida has a long history of product liability lawsuits, a deep pool of lawyers expert in product liability law and much to gain financially because its aged population suffers heavily from lung cancer and other tobacco-related illnesses, lawyers said.

Gov. Lawton Chiles is a staunch anti-tobacco activist, pushing through a 1994 law which spurred the state lawsuit and even appearing on national television shows opposing tobacco companies. He is also proposing that the state's pension fund unload all its tobacco stocks.

Hundreds of individual lawsuits are also being filed in Florida. Most come from Jacksonville lawyer Norwood Wilner, who last August won a $750,000 verdict against tobacco company Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc He represents more than 600 claims, with a trial due in April.

Wilner's victory constituted only the second loss for cigarette companies. A 1988 verdict awarding $400,000 to a New Jersey woman's estate was overturned on appeal. Brown & Williamson is expected to appeal its loss.
Tobacco companies have never been more vulnerable, experts in product liability law said.

Richard Daynard, an anti-tobocco activist and law professor who heads the Tobacco Products Liability Project at Boston's Northeastern University, said Wilner's victory last summer showed juries no longer always accept the customary industry defence that smokers choose to use tobacco products.

Tobacco defences have also been hobbled by internal tobacco documents, which have been surfacing since 1994, that appear to indicate the industry viewed cigarettes as nicotine delivery devices. The industry denies the allegations.
The flight attendants trial set for June will likely turn on scientific evidence on whether or not secondhand smoke causes lung cancer, coronary problems and other diseases, experts said.
"It's a big legal hurdle. The scientific evidence isn't mature (on secondhand smoke linkages to disease)," Eggen said. "But you can't say, 'It's your own damn fault.' These people did not smoke."

A lawyer for the flight attendants, Stanley Rosenblatt, said a negotiated settlement with the tobacco companies was nearly impossible. "In five years, not a syllable has been exchanged on that subject," he said.

Michael York, an attorney for Philip Morris Cos. Inc., the maker of Marlboro cigarettes and a defendant in many of the lawsuits, said proving the claims would be difficult and that the industry expected to win.

But speculation on Wall Street rose last week that the industry might reach a sweeping legislative compromise after RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.'s chief executive said many forces favoured a broad agreement sheltering cigarette companies from new lawsuits.
Rosenblatt, along with his attorney wife, Susan, is also handling the second Miami class action, set to go on trial Sept. 8, claiming damanges on behalf of ailing Floridians addicted to tobacco.
"Unlike the individual claims, these class-action lawsuits have the potential to bankrupt every tobacco company in the United States," Rosenblatt said.

Florida's lawsuit, claiming it is owed at least $1.1 billion for Medicaid fees paid for smokers' illnesses, is not the first of nearly 20 such cases brought by state governments scheduled to go to trial. But the high-profile case is touted by many lawyers as having a strong chance of victory for the goverment, given Florida's law.
